item.title: Books That Changed How I Think
item.dc:creator: Margaret Cole
item.description: Five books that changed how I think about my 20s, success, habits, focus and health, and what each one changed for me.
item.content:encoded:
It almost seems like a canon event that at some point in your 20s, you’ll hit a phase where you become obsessed with self-help books. I went through this phase almost a year ago, but I’ve recently had a renewed appreciation for the genre, perhaps sparked by some of my winter arc goals. So today, I’m sharing a few of my favorite books that changed how I think.

1. The Defining Decade by Meg Jay

If you read any book on this list, let it be this one. It was recommended to me by a connection I made during one of my internships. I put off reading it for several months, until it came time to start looking for jobs and I thought it might be a good strategic decision to read a few chapters before reaching back out. Once I picked it up, I literally could not stop reading. If you’re in your 20s, regardless of how successful or lost you are, this book is for you. My only regret is that I didn’t read it sooner.

Jay argues that 80% of life’s most defining moments happen by about age 35. The book is broken up into three sections (work, love, and the brain and the body), and throughout, she outlines some of the most crucial decisions you should be thinking about now, in your 20s. This book genuinely changed my life. It made me much more proactive in my decisions and forced me to seriously think about the future.

2. Outliers by Malcolm Gladwell

This book is less about what you can do to change your life and more about reframing how you view success and successful people. Gladwell argues that there is no such thing as being self-made, and that the world’s most successful people, teams, and businesses were the beneficiaries of hidden advantages. It’s also where I was introduced to the 10,000-hour rule, the idea that true expertise takes roughly 10,000 hours of practice, which has changed how I see my own growth.

3. The Power of Habit by Charles Duhigg

This book is about the science behind habit formation. Through case studies, Duhigg explores how we, as individuals, can change our habits, and how organizations can change their habits and culture as well. The examples are engaging and easy to follow, making for a great read. Beyond my own routines, it changed how I think about organizational culture and decision-making.

4. Stolen Focus by Johann Hari

This book is about the collapse of the human attention span and our inability to concentrate. Hari defines 12 factors impacting focus, such as the way algorithms are built, our diets, pollution, and stress. Each factor is relevant today and can be acted upon. It gave me a much deeper understanding of the social media algorithm and helped me break my scrolling habits.

5. Change Your Environments by Eric Berg

This was a very recent read, but I’m already implementing changes from it in my own life. Berg writes about 9 factors in our modern environment that work against our health. The book is designed to be used as a tool based on your own areas for growth, so it’s meant to be read out of order. It’s short, succinct, and actionable, and it’s helped me make small habit changes that have improved my sleep, recovery, and overall health.

None of these books handed me a perfect plan for my 20s. What they gave me is a better way of thinking about the life I’m already living. If a book has changed how you think, I’d love to hear about it, because my reading list could always use another.

This story first appeared on vitalityritual.org.
